\subsection{Verification of the closed-form model}

Every closed form in the derivation was checked against a numerical
matrix exponential and quadrature at the four delays used here.
$E_j(\delta)$ reproduces $e^{-A_c\delta}$ and $g_j(\delta)$ reproduces
$\int_0^{\delta}e^{-A_cs}B_c\,ds$ to a relative error below
$5\times10^{-16}$, and $A_d,B_d$ match \texttt{c2d} to the same order.
Two corrections were required.

\paragraph{(i) The $\omega_j$ definition.} As written,
$\omega_x=\sqrt{(q_x/2m)^2+k_x/I_x}$ mixes the plate mass into a
rotational mode; it should be $\omega_x=\sqrt{(q_x/2I_x)^2+k_x/I_x}$,
so that $\omega_j^2=\sigma_j^2+\kappa_j$ consistently. Numerically the
difference is $4\times10^{-9}$ here because $\sigma_j^2\ll\kappa_j$, so no
result changes, but the expression is still wrong as printed.
The same substitution applies to $\omega_y$. Separately, $A_c$ uses a
single $k_\theta$ for both tilts while the $\kappa$ definitions use
$k_x$ and $k_y$; the two tilt stiffnesses differ by \SI{10}{\percent}
($\SI{-7.713e-5}{}$ versus $\SI{-8.526e-5}{\newton\metre\per\radian}$)
and must be kept distinct.

\paragraph{(ii) The input index in the $z$ update.} $\Phi$ and
$\Gamma$ themselves are correct as written. The hardware schedule has
channel $i$ reaching the controller with age
$\mathrm{age}_i=t_{\mathrm{I2C}}+\Delta t_{\mathrm{ch}}(n-i+\tfrac12)$,
and for channels $1\ldots3$ that exceeds $T$, so with
$\delta_i=\mathrm{age}_i-T$,
\begin{equation}
  z[k+1]=C_i\,x(t_{k+1}-\mathrm{age}_i)=C_i\,x(t_k-\delta_i)
        =\Phi_i x[k]+\Gamma_i u[k-1]
\end{equation}
The sampling interval $[t_k-\delta_i,\,t_k]$ lies inside frame $k-1$, so
it carries $u[k-1]$, not $u[k]$ as printed. Consequently $\Gamma$
belongs in the $u[k-1]$ column of $\bar{A}_\chi$ -- which is where the
augmented system in the derivation already places it -- and not in
$\bar{B}_\chi$. The same reasoning gives $\delta_4=\mathrm{age}_4$
directly for the in-frame channel, whose row enters through
$\bar{D}u[k-1]$ exactly as written.

With this indexing the model reproduces the measurement produced by a
full nonlinear simulation of the sampler to a relative error of
$9\times10^{-4}$ once the acquisition buffer is populated.

\subsection{Weight selection}

Both gains come from a discrete Riccati solve: the regulator from
$\mathrm{dlqr}(\bar{A}_\chi,\bar{B}_\chi,Q,R)$ with
$Q=\operatorname{blkdiag}(I_6,0,0,\rho_I I_3)$ and $R=\rho_u I_3$, and
the observer from the dual $\mathrm{dlqr}(\bar{A}^\top,\bar{C}^\top,Q_o,R_o)^\top$
with $Q_o=q\,I_9$, $R_o=r\,I_4$.

The solve is performed on a \emph{non-dimensionalised} system. The raw
state mixes metres with radians and positions with rates over six
orders of magnitude, giving $\operatorname{cond}(\mathcal{C})=9.76e+11$;
after scaling each state by its characteristic magnitude this falls to
$1.28e+07$, and the observer pair from $6.98e+06$ to $1.30e+02$.

\paragraph{The binding constraints are physical, not spectral.}
Two limits dominate the choice. First, the actuator is
\emph{unilateral}: it can only pull the plate toward the electrodes,
so the most negative achievable acceleration is $-g$, while upward it
reaches $+\SI{217}{\metre\per\second\squared}$ at
$V_{\max}=\SI{120}{\volt}$. Second, the plate has only
$\pm\SI{15}{\micro\metre}$ of travel, so a transient that overshoots
that is useless however well damped it is on paper.

\paragraph{Why no weight succeeds.} The peak excursion is almost
independent of $\rho_u$, varying only between \SI{19}{} and
\SI{30}{\micro\metre} across six decades of control weight. That
insensitivity is the signature of a \emph{delay} limit rather than a
tuning one. With the plate released at $r_z=\SI{-5}{\micro\metre}$ the
open-loop mode grows as $\cosh(p_zt)$ with
$p_z=\SI{808.7}{\radian\per\second}$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lSS}
\toprule
Event & {$t$ [\si{\milli\second}]} & {$r_z$ [\si{\micro\metre}]} \\
\midrule
Channel 4 arrives & 0.59 & -6.18 \\
Channel 1 arrives & 1.13 & -9.79 \\
Plate reaches the wall & 1.54 & -15.00 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The first usable measurement lands at \SI{1.13}{\milli\second}, by which
time the plate is already at \SI{-9.8}{\micro\metre} and moving at
\SI{-9.6}{\milli\metre\per\second}; it strikes the wall
\SI{0.41}{\milli\second} later. No causal controller recovers from that,
which is consistent with $p_zt_d=0.91>1$.

The fractional-delay model is therefore necessary but not sufficient:
it makes the \emph{linear} loop stable, where a delay-ignorant design is
not, but the stabilising transient exceeds the physical travel. The
design becomes usable only once $t_d$ is reduced; at the present
$t_{\mathrm{I2C}}=\SI{500}{\micro\second}$ it is not.
